\section*{Score Advanced papers}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA01-P2-PHY-S3-Q01, source={Score Advanced - Test 01 (22 Sep 2020)}, paper=2, qno=1, type=numerical, subtopic={Gas laws}, answer={0.25}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: piston with friction on gas, gas laws | steps: force balance; pressure; isothermal change; displacement}]
As shown, a piston chamber of cross section area A is filled with ideal gas. A sealed piston of mass m is right at the middle height of the cylinder at equilibrium. The friction force between the chamber wall and the piston can be ignored. The mass of the rest of the chamber is M. The atmosphere pressure is P$_0$. Now slowly pull the piston upwards isothermally, find the maximum value of $\dfrac Mm$ such that the chamber can be lifted off the ground. Given that $\mathrm P_0=\dfrac{3mg}{2A}$\par
\bfig{139.8}{SA01_p2_phy_s3_q01_1.png}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA05-P1-PHY-S1-Q20, source={Score Advanced - Test 05 (15 Jul 2021)}, paper=1, qno=20, type=single, subtopic={Gas laws}, answer={A}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: pressure from a density against temperature graph, gas laws | steps: rho=PM/RT; read the slope at P; pressure}]
The variation of density ($\rho$) with temperature (T) of an ideal gas of molecular mass (M) at constant pressure is plotted as shown in figure. The pressure of the gas at state P will be :-\par
\bfig{96.7}{SA05_p1_phy_s1_q20_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\dfrac{\text{RT}^2}{\sqrt{3}\text{M}}$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\text{RT}^2}{\text{M}}$}
\opt{C}{$\dfrac{\text{RT}^2}{\text{M}}$}
\opt{D}{$\dfrac{\text{RT}^2}{2\text{M}}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA06-P2-PHY-S3-Q03, source={Score Advanced - Test 06 (04 Sep 2021)}, paper=2, qno=3, type=numerical, subtopic={Gas laws}, answer={215}, answer_src=solved, working={Pb=1.213e5 Pa, Pc=2.013e5 Pa; T=294 x 2.013/1.213=488 K=215 C}, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: temperature to restore the piston height, gas laws, pressures after the piston and after the man | steps: pressures after the piston and after the man; isothermal first, then constant pressure}]
A highly conducting cylinder that has cross-sectional area of 100 cm$^2$ and 50 cm deep is filled with air at 21$^\circ$C and 1.00 atm figure (a). A 20kg piston is now lowered into the cylinder, compressing the air trapped inside figure (b). Finally a 80 kg man stands on the piston, further compressing the air, which remains at 21$^\circ$C figure (c). What temperature T (in $^\circ$C) should the gas be maintained to raise the piston and the man back to h$_i$. Take g = 10m/s$^2$\par
\bfig{179.9}{SA06_p2_phy_s3_q03_1.png}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA07-P1-PHY-S3-Q03, source={Score Advanced - Test 07 (16 Apr 2023)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=numerical, subtopic={Gas laws}, answer={9}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: two gas chambers with a piston-spring system, gas laws, pressure balance through the spring force | steps: pressure balance through the spring force; PV=nRT for each chamber}]
Consider the shown diagram where the two chambers separated by piston-spring arrangement contain equal amounts of same ideal gas. Initially when the temperatures of the gas in both the chambers are kept at 300 K, the compression in the spring is 10 cm. The temperature of the left and the right chambers are now raised slowly to 400 K and 500 K respectively. The pistons are free to slide (i.e. no friction between piston and chamber). Final compression in the spring is found to be $\dfrac{\alpha}{60}$m. Find $\alpha$. (Use $\sqrt{481}$ = 22 )\par
\bfig{195.9}{SA07_p1_phy_s3_q03_1.png}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA12-P1-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score Advanced - Test 12 (11 May 2023)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=single, subtopic={Gas laws}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F0}, diff_note={concepts: piston in a cylinder of ideal gas oscillating about equilibrium, gas laws, pressure from the weight of the piston | steps: pressure from the weight of the piston; isothermal or adiabatic change}]
As shown, a piston chamber of cross section area A is filled with ideal gas. A sealed piston of mass m is right at the middle height of the cylinder at equilibrium. The friction force between the chamber wall and the piston can be ignored. The mass of the gas + chamber is M. The atmosphere pressure is P$_0$ . Now slowly pull the piston upwards, find the maximum value of M such that the chamber can be lifted off the ground. The temperature remains unchanged.\par
\bfig{81.3}{SA12_p1_phy_s1_q03_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{M = $\dfrac{\text{P}_0\text{A} - 2\text{mg}}{2\text{g}}$}
\opt{B}{M = $\dfrac{\text{P}_0\text{A} - \text{mg}}{2\text{g}}$}
\opt{C}{M = $\dfrac{\text{P}_0\text{A} - \text{mg}}{\text{g}}$}
\opt{D}{M = $\dfrac{\text{P}_0\text{A}}{2\text{g}}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA15-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score Advanced - Test 15 (18 May 2023)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=single, subtopic={Degrees of freedom}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K2 S1 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: temperature change for a process with molar specific heat 2R, degrees of freedom | steps: C=Cv+R/(1-x) gives x=-1, so PV\^{}-1 is constant and T proportional to V\^{}2}]
One mole of a monoatomic gas is heated in such a way that its molar specific heat is $2R$. If the volume of the gas is doubled, by what factor does the temperature change?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$}
\opt{B}{$\sqrt2$}
\opt{C}{2}
\opt{D}{4}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA16-P2-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score Advanced - Test 16 (20 May 2023)}, paper=2, qno=2, type=multi, subtopic={Molecular speeds}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K2 S1 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: kinetic theory statements, molecular speeds | steps: speed distribution; mean energy}]
Select the statement(s) among the following which are \textbf{correct} according to kinetic theory of gas? [All symbols have their usual meaning]
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{A molecule can have a speed greater than $\sqrt{\dfrac{6RT}{M}}$.}
\opt{B}{When the temperature of a gas is doubled, then the most probable speed is twice.}
\opt{C}{Kinetic energy of one mole of monoatomic gas is $\dfrac{3RT}{2}$.}
\opt{D}{Kinetic energy of two moles of diatomic gas is $\dfrac{5RT}{2}$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA18-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score Advanced - Test 18 (27 May 2023)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=multi, subtopic={Kinetic theory}, answer={A,B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=9, diff_parts={K3 S2 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: helium atoms in a cubical box with collision rate, kinetic theory, pressure from momentum transfer | steps: pressure from momentum transfer; rms speed; mass}]
A cubical box of side 1 meter contains helium gas (atomic weight 4) at a pressure of 100 Nm$^{-2}$. During an observation time of 1 second, it was found there are 500 collisions per helium atom perpendicular to wall. Ideal gas theory is valid in this given situation. Take $R=\frac{25}{3}$ J mol$^{-1}$k$^{-1}$ and $k=1.38\times10^{-23}$ JK$^{-1}$. Choose the correct options.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Temperature of the gas is 160 K.}
\opt{B}{Average K.E. per atom is $3.312\times10^{-21}$ J.}
\opt{C}{Total mass of helium gas in the box is $3\times10^{-4}$ kg.}
\opt{D}{Total mass of helium gas in the box is $2\times10^{-4}$ kg.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA21-P1-PHY-S1-Q05, source={Score Advanced - Test 21 (08 Apr 2024)}, paper=1, qno=5, type=multi, subtopic={Gas laws}, answer={A,B,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=9, diff_parts={K3 S2 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: gas in two compartments with a conducting movable partition, gas laws, final pressures equal | steps: final pressures equal; temperature equal; Boyle law}]
A partition divides a container having insulated walls into two compartments I and II. The same gas fills the two compartments whose initial parameters are given. The partition is a conducting wall which can move freely without friction. Which of the following statement's is/are correct, with reference to the final equilibrium position?\par
(initially the partition is held at rest)\par
\bfig{106.3}{SA21_p1_phy_s1_q05_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The Pressure in the two compartments are equal.}
\opt{B}{Volume of compartment I is $\dfrac{3V}{5}$}
\opt{C}{Volume of compartment II is $\dfrac{12V}{5}$}
\opt{D}{Final pressure in compartment I is $\dfrac{5P}{3}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA24-P1-PHY-S1-Q01, source={Score Advanced - Test 24 (17 Apr 2024)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=multi, subtopic={Gas laws}, answer={B,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: ideal gas in two connected cylinders with pistons, gas laws, pressure balance on each piston | steps: pressure balance on each piston; equal pressure and temperature}]
Two vertical conducting cylinders A and B of different cross sections are connected by a thin tube as shown. An ideal gas is trapped in the cylinders by two airtight pistons of masses 1.0 kg and 2.0 kg respectively. Initially the pistons are at the same height 40 cm above the base of the cylinders. If an additional mass of 10 g were gently placed on the piston in the cylinder A, which of the following statements correctly describe the new steady state ultimately reached.\par
\bfig{76.8}{SA24_p1_phy_s1_q01_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Pressure of the gas has been increased.}
\opt{B}{Pressure of the gas remains unchanged.}
\opt{C}{Height difference between the pistons becomes 30 cm.}
\opt{D}{Height difference between the pistons becomes 60 cm.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SA27-P1-PHY-S2-Q10, source={Score Advanced - Test 27 (24 Apr 2024)}, paper=1, qno=10, type=multi, subtopic={Kinetic theory}, answer={A,B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: two boxes of ideal gas at equal temperature, kinetic theory, equal mean kinetic energy per molecule | steps: equal mean kinetic energy per molecule}]
We have two equal size boxes A and B. Each box contains gas that behaves as an ideal gas. Thermometer are inserted into each box and it is found that the gas in box A is at a temperature of 50$^\circ$C, while the gas in box B is at 10$^\circ$C. Which of the following statements(s) is/are true?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The pressure in A may be higher than in B.}
\opt{B}{There may be more molecules in A and than in B.}
\opt{C}{The molecules in A have more average kinetic energy per molecule than those in B.}
\opt{D}{The molecules in A are moving faster than B.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
